what: The Image Compressor makes photos and pictures smaller in file size so they load faster, upload faster and take less space. It works by saving the picture again as a JPG or WebP file at the quality you choose, and it can also make the picture narrower if it is wider than you need.

It is useful for anyone who has to send or post images: bloggers and shop owners who want faster pages, students who must upload a photo under a size limit, and anyone whose email or chat app refuses a large file. You can see the new size and the percentage saved before you download.
The whole job happens inside your browser. Your image is never sent to a server, so private photos stay on your device.
uses: Large photos are the main reason pages load slowly. Compress them to a few hundred KB before you upload them to your site or online shop.
Many forms only accept photos under 1 MB or 200 KB. Lower the quality and set a max width until the "Compressed" size fits.
Send photos by email or chat
Phone photos are often 3 to 6 MB. Compressing them first means they attach faster and use less mobile data.
Shrink an archive of screenshots or scans so they take less room on your phone, laptop or cloud drive.
Choose WebP as the output format to get a smaller file than JPG at the same visual quality, which is good for the web.
tutorial: Click the box that says "Click or drop an image here", or drag a file onto it. JPG, PNG and WebP files work best. The tool compresses it straight away with the default settings.
Under the settings you will see "Original", "Compressed" and "Saved". Saved is the percentage of file size you removed. Below the preview, a short line shows the final width and height in pixels.
The "Quality" slider goes from 10% to 95% and starts at 70%. Lower numbers give smaller files but more blur and blocky edges. The preview and sizes update every time you move it.
In "Output format" pick JPG or WebP. JPG opens everywhere. WebP is usually 20 to 30% smaller at the same quality and works in all modern browsers, but some older programs cannot open it.
Set a max width if you need it

Type a number in "Max width (px, optional)", for example 1600. If the image is wider than this, it is scaled down and the height changes in proportion. Leave it empty to keep the original size. A smaller width saves far more space than a lower quality.
Look at the preview image, especially faces, small text and sharp edges. If it looks blurry or blocky, raise the quality a little until it looks right to you.
Click "Download image". The file is saved with "-compressed" added to the name, for example holiday-compressed.jpg. Your original file is not changed.
features: Every change to quality, format or width redraws the image at once, so you can see the result before saving.
Shows the original size, the new size and the percent saved, so you know exactly what you gained.
A simple slider controls how hard the image is compressed. 60 to 80% is the usual sweet spot for photos.
Save in the most common format or in the smaller modern WebP format.
Scale a large photo down to a sensible width in the same step, keeping its shape.
Compression uses your browser’s own image engine, with no upload and no account.

example.title: Worked example: shrinking a phone photo for a blog
example.text: You have a phone photo that is 4000 × 3000 px and 4.1 MB. You drop it in, leave Quality at 70% and Output format on JPG, and type 1600 in Max width. The picture becomes 1600 × 1200 px, because 3000 × 1600 ÷ 4000 = 1200. The Compressed box shows a size of roughly 250 to 400 KB, so Saved reads about 90%. You check the preview, it looks sharp on screen, and you click "Download image" to get photo-compressed.jpg.

tips: Try a smaller max width before you push the quality very low. Halving the width cuts the file to about a quarter.
For screen use, 1200 to 2000 px wide is enough for almost every website and chat app.
Keep your original file. Compression removes detail that cannot be brought back later.
Choose WebP for websites you control, and JPG when you are not sure the other person can open WebP.
Do not compress the same JPG again and again. Each save loses a little more quality, so always start from the original.
problems: The message says the image is already well compressed and Saved shows 0%

The new file came out the same size or bigger, so the button changes to "Download original" and gives you your untouched file instead of a bigger one. To get a smaller file, lower the Quality slider, set a Max width, or try WebP instead of JPG.
JPG cannot store transparency, so empty areas are filled with white. Choose WebP in Output format to keep the see-through areas.
Text or a logo looks fuzzy
Sharp graphics suffer most from compression. Raise the quality to 85% or more, or keep that image as a PNG and do not compress it here.
The file you chose is not an image, for example a PDF or a document. Pick a JPG, PNG or WebP file.
"Your browser could not encode this format"
Your browser cannot save WebP. Switch Output format to JPG, or update your browser.
